blocks.text: The **CPU (Central Processing Unit)**, also called the **processor**, is the main hardware unit that executes program instructions and coordinates processing. It is often described as the **brain** of the computer. The CPU directly executes **machine language**: instructions encoded as binary 0s and 1s. High-level programs must ultimately be translated into machine instructions.

blocks.title: Three basic parts of the CPU
rows: Decodes instructions and directs operations. It fetches and decodes instructions, issues control signals, and coordinates registers, memory and input/output interfaces.
Provides very fast temporary storage inside the CPU.

blocks.title: Control, not calculation
blocks.text: The control unit **controls** calculations; it does not do the arithmetic itself. The ALU calculates. Some elementary books call internal storage the **Memory Unit (MU)**, but RAM is separate main memory. 'Program unit' is **not** a standard CPU component.

blocks.title: Memory trick
blocks.text: **CU directs; ALU calculates; registers hold the immediate values.** The CPU is hardware: it is the processor, not the whole computer box.

blocks.title: Instruction cycle
items: Perform it in the relevant execution unit

blocks.title: The four stages
items: **Decode:** identify the operation that is needed.
**Execute:** perform the operation using the relevant execution unit.
**Write back:** save a result when one has to be stored.

blocks.text: **Device installation** is not a stage of the instruction cycle, although installation software still uses CPU cycles like any other program.

blocks.title: How the CPU, memory and I/O work together
items: **Memory** holds the programs and data being worked on.
The **control unit** coordinates all these transfers.

blocks.text: The **ALU (Arithmetic Logic Unit)** is a major building block of the CPU. It processes **operands** (the values to work on) under control signals from the Control Unit and returns a result.

blocks.title: Two functional sections of the ALU
rows: Numerical calculations such as addition and subtraction. Multiplication and division may use dedicated circuits or sequences of simpler operations.

blocks.title: Logical operations
items: **AND, OR and NOT** act on binary values.
Comparisons test **equal to, greater than and less than**.
These operations support selecting, matching, sorting and merging data; such complete tasks normally need several instructions.

blocks.title: A precise view of execution
blocks.text: The ALU executes arithmetic and logical operations; **other execution units** handle other instruction types. So not every instruction is performed entirely by the ALU. Comparing data is a **logic** task.

blocks.title: Accumulator and advanced maths
rows: A CPU **register** used in some architectures to hold an operand or an intermediate arithmetic or logical result. Other designs keep results in general-purpose registers. It is a register, not a separate kind of main memory.
May be handled by a **Floating-Point Unit (FPU)**, other specialised circuits, or software routines.
Does not necessarily have dedicated hardware for every advanced mathematical function.

blocks.text: Two ALU sections: arithmetic and logic. Intermediate results are held in registers.

**Registers** are small, extremely fast storage locations inside a processor. They temporarily hold operands, instructions, addresses and intermediate results. They are generally faster to access than cache or RAM, but they are **temporary working storage, not permanent storage**.
A register is a **sequential digital circuit**, usually made from **flip-flops**. Each flip-flop stores **one bit**, so an **n-bit register holds n bits** (bit 0, bit 1 ... bit n-1).

blocks.title: Important registers
rows: Memory Address Register: holds the address of the main-memory location to be read or written.
Memory Data Register, also called Memory Buffer Register: holds data being transferred to or from memory.
Program Counter: holds the address used to locate the next instruction.
Instruction Register: holds the instruction being decoded or executed.

blocks.title: Memory trick
blocks.text: **MAR = address; MDR/MBR = transferred data; PC = next instruction; IR = current instruction.** MAR holds a memory address; it does not fetch disk data directly.

A **buffer** temporarily holds data during a transfer. It helps devices or components exchange data when their operating rates differ. A **buffer register** provides this temporary storage in a data path, for example between a faster and a slower component.

blocks.title: Main and secondary memory
rows: Holds programs and data currently in use. CPU access normally passes through a memory hierarchy that includes cache.
Retain data for longer periods. Data is normally loaded into RAM before the CPU processes it.

blocks.text: Registers are the fastest among registers, cache and main memory. A **stack** is a way of organising data, not a separate memory technology with a fixed speed.

**Clock speed** is the number of CPU clock cycles per second. Clock frequency is measured in **hertz (Hz)**, where 1 Hz is one cycle per second. A 3 GHz clock produces about 3 billion cycles per second.

blocks.title: Instruction throughput
rows: Kilo Instructions Per Second: thousands of instructions per second. 100 KIPS = 100,000 instructions per second.
Million Instructions Per Second. 1 MIPS = 1,000,000 instructions per second = 1,000 KIPS.

blocks.title: Clock period
rows: Frequency = 1 / clock period. A shorter clock period means a higher clock frequency.
For otherwise comparable designs this may improve speed, but frequency alone does not decide performance.

blocks.title: Cycles are not instructions
blocks.text: Some instructions take several cycles, and some processors complete several instructions in one cycle. Architecture, instructions per cycle, core count, cache, memory and workload all affect performance.

blocks.title: Important corrections
items: There is no universal personal-computer speed of 100 KIPS.
**Hz** measures clock frequency; **KIPS and MIPS** describe instruction throughput.
MIPS is not a reliable universal comparison across different instruction sets.
Bits or bytes per second measure **data-transfer rate**, while KB, GB and TB describe **data capacity**.

blocks.title: Instruction-set approaches
rows: Simpler, regular instruction designs and efficient execution
Supports more complex instruction forms and operations
Traditional designs can need more elaborate instruction decoding
Arm is a RISC architecture family
Not automatically costlier; cost depends on the full implementation

blocks.text: CISC is **not automatically more costly** in every case; complexity and manufacturing cost depend on the full implementation. RISC and CISC describe instruction-set approaches, not core counts.

blocks.title: Memory trick
blocks.text: **R**educed = **R**egular and simple; **C**omplex = **C**ompound, many-step instructions.
A **core** is a processing unit inside a CPU. Multiple cores can execute work at the same time when the software and tasks permit.

These are only examples, not the only possible core counts. Single-core designs appeared **before** dual-core, triple-core and quad-core processors, and the Intel 4004 was an early single-core microprocessor.

blocks.title: Core count is not a brand name
blocks.text: A **dual-core** CPU has two cores; it need not belong to the Intel Core 2 product family.

blocks.title: Uniprocessor and multiprocessor
rows: Traditionally a system with one CPU.
Traditionally a system with multiple CPUs.
Different things: one CPU package can contain several cores.
Concerns execution threads and is not a synonym for multiple physical processors.

blocks.text: A **microprocessor** implements CPU processing functions on an **integrated circuit**. Microprocessor-based computers belong to the **fourth generation** in the usual textbook classification.

blocks.title: Key processor facts
rows: Widely recognised as the first commercially available single-chip microprocessor. It was a 4-bit processor.
A 16-bit processor with a 16-bit external data bus and a 20-bit physical address.

blocks.title: Processor companies
rows: The name was formed from 'integrated electronics'.
Advanced Micro Devices. Both companies develop processors, and AMD also develops graphics processors.

blocks.title: Intel 8086 specifications
rows: Combines segment and offset values to form a physical address.

blocks.text: Word size and address width are different specifications: the 8086 has a **16-bit** word but a **20-bit** physical address.

blocks.title: ARM at a glance
rows: ARM originally meant **Acorn RISC Machine**; **Advanced RISC Machine** is a commonly taught later expansion.
Founded as Advanced RISC Machines Ltd.
The Arm architecture originated at **Acorn Computers**.
The ARM1 chip worked in **1985**; early uses included Acorn computer systems.
A **RISC** architecture family (Reduced Instruction Set Computer).

blocks.text: Energy-efficient Arm designs are widely used in **phones, tablets and embedded devices**. They were not originally created exclusively for mobile systems.
Intel 4004 = 1971, 4-bit. 8086 = 16-bit word, 20-bit physical address. Arm = RISC heritage and energy efficiency.

A **GPU (Graphics Processing Unit)** is a specialised processor originally developed to speed up **graphics rendering**. It handles many similar calculations **in parallel**, which makes it useful for graphics and other suitable workloads.

blocks.title: Main applications
items: Smartphones also contain GPUs, usually integrated into a **system-on-chip** along with CPU cores and other parts.

blocks.title: CPU vs GPU
rows: General-purpose instruction execution, coordination and flexible, control-heavy tasks
Many parallel arithmetic operations for workloads that can be split into similar calculations

blocks.title: GPU vs graphics card
rows: An add-in board containing a GPU plus supporting parts such as video memory, power circuitry and cooling.
Need not be on a separate graphics card.

blocks.title: History: careful wording
items: Sony's original PlayStation used a graphics processor; the source material associates the GPU term with Sony.
NVIDIA's GeForce 256 was a major consumer GPU milestone.

blocks.text: These facts do not show that one company invented all graphics-processing technology. CPUs and GPUs often work together; CPUs can also do parallel work, and GPUs are **not faster for every task**.

The **case, cabinet or chassis** is the enclosure that houses a desktop computer's main internal components. The assembled case with its contents is commonly called the **system unit**. It typically contains the motherboard, CPU, RAM, storage drives, power supply and cooling.
'CPU cabinet' is an informal phrase. The CPU is the **processor**, not the entire box.

blocks.title: Power supply
rows: Switched-Mode Power Supply, also written Switch-Mode Power Supply.
Power Supply Unit: converts incoming **AC** electricity into regulated **DC** power for computer components.
Its circuits can further regulate voltages for individual chips.
The PSU is a separate component in the cabinet, not inside the CPU chip.

blocks.title: Offline devices
rows: In traditional usage, a device that is unavailable for direct communication with, or control by, the computer.
It may be disconnected, switched off or otherwise unavailable; offline does not necessarily mean faulty.
Offline can mean disconnected from a network or the internet.

blocks.text: Buses are the pathways that carry **addresses, data and control signals** between the CPU and memory or other devices.

blocks.title: Three basic system buses
rows: Carries the address that identifies a memory location or device.
Carries signals such as read, write and timing or control information.

blocks.title: The cache-bus question
blocks.text: **Address, data and control** are the standard three categories. A 'cache bus' is outside this basic classification, although specialised cache interconnects can exist.
Case houses components; CPU executes instructions; SMPS supplies regulated power; buses carry addresses, data and control signals.

revision: CPU (Central Processing Unit) is the processor, the main hardware unit that executes instructions; it runs machine language made of 0s and 1s.
CPU parts: Control Unit directs, ALU calculates and compares, registers hold immediate values; the control unit does not do arithmetic.
Instruction cycle: fetch, decode, execute, write back; device installation is not a stage.
ALU has an arithmetic section (add, subtract and so on) and a logic section (comparisons, AND, OR, NOT).
An accumulator is a register that holds an operand or intermediate result; it is not main memory.
MAR = address in memory; MDR/MBR = data to or from memory; PC = next instruction address; IR = current instruction.
Registers are made of flip-flops (1 bit each) and are the fastest storage: registers, then cache, then RAM, then disk.
1 GHz = 1,000 MHz = 1 billion cycles per second; 1 MIPS = 1,000 KIPS; frequency = 1 / clock period.
Hz measures clock frequency; KIPS and MIPS measure instruction throughput; bits or bytes per second measure data transfer.
RISC = Reduced Instruction Set Computer (simpler instructions, Arm); CISC = Complex Instruction Set Computer.
Core counts: single 1, dual 2, quad 4, hexa 6, octa 8, deca 10; a dual-core CPU is not the same as Intel Core 2.
Intel 4004 (1971) was the first commercial single-chip microprocessor, a 4-bit processor; microprocessors define the fourth generation.
Intel 8086: 16-bit word, 16-bit data bus, 20-bit physical address, so 1 MiB (1,048,576 bytes) addressable.
ARM originally meant Acorn RISC Machine; the ARM1 chip worked in 1985 and Arm designs are energy efficient.
GPU = Graphics Processing Unit, strong at parallel work; a graphics card is a board that contains a GPU.
Three system buses: address, data and control; SMPS/PSU converts AC to regulated DC power.
